This is the GPU that will be used for rendering, when Use GPU if available is selected. If you have more than one GPU in your machine, you can select a different GPU Device to use by editing your Preferences. (Note that selecting a different GPU will require a restart of Nuke to take effect.) Local GPU will be shown as Not available when any of the following is true: * Use CPU is selected as the GPU Device in your Preferences. * No suitable GPU was found on your system. Please refer to the documentation for details of the requirements for GPU acceleration. * It was not possible to create a context for processing on the selected GPU. For example, this can happen when there is not enough free memory available on the GPU. To use the GPU when rendering from the command line, add --gpu to your command.

Whether to normalize the results to compensate for tearing (holes appearing behind moving objects) and collisions (objects moving on top of one another) in the rendered output.

Normalizing can exacerbate the effects of tearing and collisions, but it tends to give a softer blur than not normalizing. Which to use will depend on both your input and the desired effect.

Select this to render on the Local GPU, if available. You can select this even if no GPU is currently available on your machine. The GPU will then be used whenever the script is opened on a machine which does have a GPU available. You should also select this if you wish to render from the command line with the --gpu option. If this node requires full frames from its inputs, and is therefore unable to reduce its memory overhead, it will fall back to the CPU if an attempt to render a frame on the GPU fails due to lack of memory. When this occurs, a warning message will be printed to the console.
The u channel controls the horizontal size of the blur vector, the v channel controls the vertical size. @i;If uv's are read from a file, be sure to set the read colorspace to raw data.
Constant value added to the u and v. For uv data read from a file this should be -.5 or possibly -127/255.

description.plain_text: VectorBlur: Blurs each pixel into a straight line, using the values of the u and v channels to determine the direction to blur in. The main use of this is to add Motion Blur to an image. Many renderers can be made to produce this motion data as a 2-channel floating-point image. You should unpremult these images if possible. The MotionBlur3D operator can be used to produce vectors from an animated Nuke Camera operator. Use ChannelCopy to put them into the uv channels of the rendering, then use this operator to add the motion blur. You can also use the constant values to add motion blur for camera movement and shake. Subtract the x/y translate or camera rotation at this frame from frame+1 to get the correct values.
